passage: The panel had twenty minutes to choose between two final candidates, and the manager was already late for a flight. Mahima, twenty-five, noticed her pen hovering over the first name: a graduate of her own college, whose professors she knew and whose jokes she'd laughed at. The other, Sharmila, came from the rival college whose students had booed Mahima's team at every fest. Mahima felt the tug, warm and familiar. She put the pen down. "Let me check the scores again," she said. On the case exercise, Sharmila was stronger by a clear margin. Mahima reminded herself they would all be on one team now: same city office, same clients. "Sharmila," she said. The manager nodded and left for the airport. Walking back, Mahima still felt proud of her old college. It just didn't get to choose for her.

qa.q: How long did the panel have to choose?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Mahima feel when her pen hovered over the first name?
qa.a: She felt a warm, familiar tug to favour a graduate of her own college.

qa.q: What choice did Mahima make, and what helped her make it fairly?
qa.a: She rechecked the scores and chose Sharmila, reminding herself they would all be on one team, in the same office, with the same clients.

qa.q: How would things have changed for Sharmila if Mahima had followed the tug?
qa.a: Sharmila, the stronger candidate, would have lost the job because of an old college rivalry rather than her work.

grounding: A young panellist notices the pull to favour her own college, turns to the wider shared identity of one team, and judges an outsider fairly while keeping her pride.

passage: The two blocks of the Hebbal apartment complex had never got along: Block A said Block B's kids were rough, Block B said A's were spoilt. Vishal, twenty-six and the new father of a toddler, caught himself nodding along at an A-block meeting. Then one evening at the park his daughter tripped, and it was Usha from Block B who scooped her up and dusted her knees before he could get there. Usha's son had the same scab on the same knee. They both laughed. Sitting on the bench, Vishal realised they were just two tired parents in the same park. At the next A-block meeting, when someone said, "B people never pay maintenance on time," Vishal said, "Let's check the records before we say that." He suggested a joint parents' group for the play area. Some grumbled. Twelve families joined.

qa.q: Who scooped up Vishal's daughter when she tripped?
qa.a: Usha from Block B.

qa.q: What did Vishal realise on the bench with Usha?
qa.a: That they were just two tired parents in the same park, not rivals from different blocks.

qa.q: What choices did Vishal make at the next A-block meeting?
qa.a: He asked to check the records before blaming B people, and suggested a joint parents' group for the play area.

qa.q: How might Usha see Block A after this?
qa.a: Usha may feel the divide soften, having been treated as a fellow parent rather than as one of the 'B people'.

grounding: A young father notices his pull toward his own block, finds a wider shared identity as a parent, and pushes for fairness toward the other block.

passage: "Papa, the Menons want to rent the upstairs flat." Bhupen frowned over his newspaper. "Menons? Not from here. Better to give it to someone from our own people." Sabina put down her tea. "Papa, when you came to Guwahati for your job, weren't you 'not from here' too?" "That was different." "How?" "We... fitted in." "Because Mr Barua's family gave you a chance. You've told me that story a hundred times." Bhupen was silent. "Mr Menon teaches at my college. They have a baby. They've paid the deposit on time for every flat they've rented." "And if they're noisy?" "Then we talk to them, same as we'd talk to anyone." Bhupen folded the paper slowly. "Call them for tea on Sunday. Both families."

qa.q: Where does Mr Menon teach?
qa.a: At Sabina's college.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's silence after Sabina's reminder suggest?
qa.a: He seems uncomfortable, recognising that he was once an outsider given a chance and that his objection doesn't hold up.

qa.q: Which of Sabina's arguments changed Bhupen's mind, and why?
qa.a: Reminding him that Mr Barua's family gave him a chance when he was new, which widened 'our own people' to anyone who once needed a start.

qa.q: What would change for the Menons if Bhupen had refused?
qa.a: The Menons, a family with a baby and a good record, would lose a home simply for not being 'from here'.

grounding: A young woman helps her father move past favouring 'our own people' by recalling a wider shared identity as newcomers, so an outsider family is treated fairly.

passage: I'm Ujjwal. Last year our small software firm was bought by a bigger one, and suddenly there were "old" people and "new" people on the same floor. I'm from the old side. For the first month I ate lunch only with my old team. When a new colleague missed a deadline, I heard myself say, "Typical new lot." Nobody said it was wrong, which made it worse. Then Kishore, from the new side, stayed back till ten helping me fix a server crash that wasn't even his. "Go home, bhai, I'll watch the logs," he said at one point, and I didn't. Walking to the auto stand, we realised we lived in the same part of town and supported the same cricket team. The next morning I split our project tasks by skill, not by which company people came from. I'm still proud of what our old team built. I just stopped needing the new people to be worse.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal hear himself say when a new colleague missed a deadline?
qa.a: He heard himself say, 'Typical new lot.'

qa.q: What did Ujjwal realise about his own attitude, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ujjwal realised the old team was being favoured, shown by eating lunch only with them, and felt uneasy that nobody challenged the 'Typical new lot' remark.

qa.q: Which choice by Ujjwal treated people more fairly, and why did it help?
qa.a: Splitting project tasks by skill rather than by company judged everyone on their work, which loosened the old-versus-new line.

qa.q: How might Kishore see Ujjwal after that night fixing the server?
qa.a: Kishore might see him as a colleague and neighbour rather than someone from the other side, and feel more at home on the floor.

grounding: After a merger a young adult catches himself favouring his old team, finds shared ground with a new colleague and treats both sides fairly, keeping pride without contempt.

passage:
League coordinator's note, 14 October. Written by Ms Kaur.

Chinmay, twenty-four, volunteers as an assistant referee and still plays for Northside FC. Today he was assigned Northside against Eastbank, their fiercest rivals. I watched him closely. When a Northside player went down near the box, the Northside bench screamed for a penalty. Chinmay kept his flag down: it was a clean tackle. His old teammates booed him. Afterwards, Eshaan, the Eastbank captain, came over to thank him. Chinmay said, "You'd get the same from me any day. We're all the same league." Then he suggested something I had never heard from either side: a joint training morning for the under-twelves of both clubs.

My next step: I've booked the ground for that morning and asked Chinmay and Eshaan to run it together.

qa.q: Which teams played in the match Chinmay helped referee?
qa.a: Northside FC played Eastbank, their fiercest rivals.

qa.q: What did Chinmay seem to be thinking when he kept his flag down despite the booing?
qa.a: He seemed focused on being fair to both sides and willing to accept his teammates' anger rather than favour his own club.

qa.q: Why was suggesting a joint training morning a good next step?
qa.a: It builds a wider shared identity, one league and one set of young players, so the rivalry does not turn into contempt.

qa.q: How might Northside players feel about Chinmay after the match?
qa.a: Some may feel betrayed at first, but over time they might trust that he calls games honestly, including when it helps them.

grounding: A young volunteer referee resists favouring his own club, treats the rival fairly and builds a wider shared identity across clubs.

passage:
Wednesday night
Baby Aarohi finally asleep. Writing fast.
In the society park this morning, I noticed it again: the Marathi mothers on one bench, the North Indian mothers on the other. I always sit with the Marathi group. They're my people, we joke in our language. Today Vidya from the other bench was struggling with her twins, one crying, one running at the road. My first thought, honestly, was "not my group." I hated that I thought it.
I went over and grabbed the runaway twin. Vidya looked like she'd cry with relief. We ended up talking about sleepless nights and teething, and it turned out we're both terrified of the same things.
Tomorrow I'm going to sit on her bench. Still proud of my group. But we're all mothers here first, aren't we?
- Rekha

qa.q: What was Vidya struggling with?
qa.a: Vidya was struggling with her twins, one crying, one running at the road.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel about the first thought of "not my group"?
qa.a: Rekha felt ashamed and uncomfortable, hating having thought it.

qa.q: What wider identity helps Rekha, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Seeing everyone as mothers first gives a shared identity that lets Rekha keep pride in her group while treating Vidya fairly.

qa.q: How might Vidya have felt when Rekha grabbed the runaway twin?
qa.a: Vidya felt enormous relief and gratitude, looking like she might cry.

grounding: A young mother notices the pull to favour her own group, finds a wider identity as fellow parents, and treats another mother fairly while keeping her pride.

passage: In their village near Mandya, the two hamlets had played separate cricket teams for years, and every match ended in taunts. Jaya, twenty-four, the new schoolteacher, grew up in the upper hamlet and still cheered loudest for it. But when the district tournament was announced, she noticed something: each hamlet team was too small to compete alone. At the temple meeting she said, "What if we play as one team, the village team?" Pankaj, captain of the lower hamlet, crossed his arms. "Your side always thinks it's better." Jaya nodded. "Maybe we do. I still love my hamlet. But the district team won't care which lane we live in." She suggested the captaincy alternate between hamlets. Two months later, the combined team reached the district semifinal. Jaya still wore her hamlet's scarf. She just cheered for everyone now.

qa.q: What round did the combined team reach?
qa.a: The combined team reached the district semifinal.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when Pankaj said her side always thinks it's better?
qa.a: Jaya felt uncomfortable but honest, admitting her bias while still proud of her hamlet.

qa.q: Which choice helped the hamlets work together, and why?
qa.a: Forming one village team with alternating captaincy created a shared identity and fairness, so rivalry gave way to cooperation.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have seen the idea of a combined team at first?
qa.a: Pankaj was suspicious and defensive, expecting the upper hamlet to act superior.

grounding: A young adult notices the pull to favour her hamlet, builds a wider village identity, and treats the other side fairly while keeping her pride.

passage:
Every Saturday, the Manchester library playgroup split in two. Parents from the new flats sat on one side, and parents from the old terraces sat on the other. Tariq, twenty-five, with his daughter on his knee, sat with the flats side.
He noticed himself smirking when a terrace dad let his son eat biscuits off the floor. Then he noticed the smirk.
Next week he sat in the middle. The terrace dad, Emeka, was struggling with a buggy. Tariq held the door.
"Never slept past five either?" Emeka asked.
"Not once in a year."
They laughed. By spring, both sides shared one big mat. Everyone had the same tired eyes and the same crying toddlers.

qa.q: Where did Tariq sit the next week?
qa.a: He sat in the middle.

qa.q: What might Tariq have felt when he noticed his own smirk?
qa.a: He likely felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, seeing that he had been judging someone just for being from the other side.

qa.q: What helped the two sides of the playgroup come together?
qa.a: Tariq sat in the middle, held the door and found a shared identity with Emeka as tired parents, which others followed.

qa.q: What is it like for Emeka when Tariq holds the door?
qa.a: Emeka feels seen and welcomed, and he responds with a joke that connects them as parents.

grounding: Shows a young father noticing his pull to look down on another group, then finding a shared identity as parents and treating the other side fairly.

passage:
The day-shift and night-shift teams at the Pune hospital lab didn't like each other. Day blamed night for dirty equipment. Night blamed day for missing samples.
Ojas, twenty-four and on day shift, caught himself saying "those night people" at lunch. He stopped.
That week he stayed an hour after his shift and met Gautam from night shift. They found the missing samples were a labelling problem, not laziness. Ojas suggested a joint handover notebook and a single notice board by the door, with both teams' names on the top: "Lab Team."
At the next staff meeting, when someone grumbled about nights, Ojas said, "We're the same lab. Gautam's team fixed half of this."

qa.q: What did the missing samples turn out to be?
qa.a: They turned out to be a labelling problem, not laziness.

qa.q: What might Ojas have felt when he caught himself saying "those night people"?
qa.a: He probably felt uneasy and embarrassed, noticing how easily he had fallen into blaming the other team.

qa.q: What small step helped the two shifts work together?
qa.a: A joint handover notebook and a notice board headed "Lab Team" gave both shifts one shared identity and a fair way to share information.

qa.q: How might Gautam see Ojas staying an hour after his shift?
qa.a: Gautam may feel respected and surprised, since someone from the day shift came to understand the night team rather than blame it.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing his pull to favour his own shift, building a wider shared identity as one lab and treating the other team fairly.

passage:
Dear Farhan,
Our school teams played again yesterday and, as usual, there was booing from both sides. My students called yours "posh kids," and I heard yours call mine "government school types." I laughed at first. I'm not proud of that.
I've coached our team for two years, and I love them fiercely. But I don't want that love to mean treating your boys as enemies.
What if our teams practised together once a month? Same city, same heat, same dusty ground at the maidan. We could mix the players in drills and share one water cooler.
I'll bring the cones if you bring the balls.
Warmly,
Damini

qa.q: What did Damini's students call Farhan's students?
qa.a: They called them "posh kids."

qa.q: How does Damini seem to feel about having laughed at first?
qa.a: Damini feels uncomfortable and a bit ashamed about laughing at the booing.

qa.q: What would you advise Farhan to do with Damini's idea?
qa.a: Farhan could agree to a monthly joint practice with mixed drills, so the players start to see each other as fellow players from the same city.

qa.q: How might the students of both teams feel after mixing in drills?
qa.a: They might feel less hostile and more curious about each other, seeing the other side as players, not enemies.

grounding: Shows a young coach who loves their own team noticing the us-and-them booing, and proposing shared practice as players from the same city.

passage: You asked about the football club. Okay. I'm Tenzin, I'm twenty-four, and when I started coaching the kids' team in our Delhi colony, I only wanted Tibetan boys. It felt natural. My people, my language, my pride. Then Sachin, a Punjabi boy from the next lane, came every evening and stood by the fence. Good feet. I kept saying 'next season'. One day I caught myself thinking, he's not one of us. And I felt ashamed, because that's exactly what people have said about us. So I changed the idea of 'us'. We became the colony team: anyone from these lanes. Sachin plays left wing now. The Tibetan boys still sing our songs before matches, and now Sachin knows them too. I'm still proud of where I come from. I just don't need anyone to be less for that.

qa.q: Where does Sachin play now?
qa.a: Left wing.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel on catching the thought 'he's not one of us'?
qa.a: Tenzin felt ashamed, knowing people had said the same about Tibetans.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do to widen the shared identity?
qa.a: He made the club the colony team, open to anyone from the lanes, keeping Tibetan pride without excluding others.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt standing by the fence every evening?
qa.a: Sachin probably felt hopeful but left out, waiting for a chance that kept being put off.

grounding: A young coach notices the pull to favour his own community and widens 'us' to the whole colony while keeping his pride.

passage: I'm Hansa, and I've sat in the same open office as Tejas since our two companies merged last year. For months it was 'us' and 'them': the old Pune team and the Mumbai lot, different lunch tables, jokes in the group chat. Tejas was one of the loudest Pune voices at first. Then something shifted. At a planning meeting I watched him catch himself mid-joke about 'Mumbai slowness', stop and say, 'Actually, we're one team now, and your data saved us last quarter.' The next week he started a Friday cricket match: mixed sides, drawn from a hat. When someone from Pune mocked a Mumbai colleague's accent, Tejas said, 'Not here.' I don't know what changed in his head. But the lunch tables have been pushed together since March.

qa.q: How are the Friday cricket sides chosen?
qa.a: Mixed sides, drawn from a hat.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling when he stopped mid-joke?
qa.a: Tejas perhaps felt a flash of discomfort or shame, noticing the pull to mock the other group.

qa.q: Which of Tejas's actions best widened the shared identity?
qa.a: Calling everyone one team, crediting the Mumbai data, mixing the cricket sides and stopping mockery with 'Not here'.

qa.q: How has Hansa's view of the office changed?
qa.a: Hansa has watched 'us and them' fade, noticing the lunch tables pushed together since March.

grounding: A colleague watches a young man loosen an office us-them split by building a shared team identity and stopping mockery.

passage:
September: at his daughter's school in Pune, Tushar joined the parents' chats and found two: one for Marathi-speaking parents, one for everyone else. He joined the Marathi one, felt at home, and laughed along at jokes about 'outsider' parents who never volunteered.
October: at sports day, the 'outsider' dad, Shankar, was the one fixing the broken microphone, running the water station and carrying Tushar's own daughter to first aid when she scraped her knee. Tushar stood with his coffee, uneasy.
December: Tushar proposed merging the chats into one, 'Class 1B parents'. A few grumbled. He posted in Marathi, Hindi and English, thanked Shankar publicly for sports day, and set a rule: no jokes about anyone's home state. By the Christmas party, Shankar and Tushar were co-organising the snacks, arguing happily about vada pav versus samosas.

qa.q: What did Shankar do at sports day?
qa.a: Fixed the broken microphone, ran the water station and carried Tushar's daughter to first aid.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he stood with his coffee at sports day?
qa.a: Tushar felt uneasy and a little ashamed, seeing the 'outsider' he had laughed at helping his own daughter.

qa.q: Which step best widened the us-them line?
qa.a: Merging the chats into one 'Class 1B parents' group with a no-jokes rule, which built a shared identity as parents.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel being thanked publicly?
qa.a: Shankar would likely feel recognised and welcomed, no longer treated as an outsider.

grounding: Over a term a young father notices his in-group favouritism and builds a wider identity of fellow parents.

passage: Sunaina, you asked why your Tanvir mama never lets anyone at the shop talk about "those people". Let me tell you. I was twenty-five, waiting outside the maternity ward at the government hospital for your cousin Rubel to be born. The corridor was split: Bengali-speaking fathers on one bench, Hindi-speaking ones on the other, and I sat with my own without thinking. I even felt a little proud of our bench. Then the power went out at midnight. A Bihari man, Ramdeo, had the only torch. He walked it down the whole corridor so every nurse could see, then shared his flask of tea with our bench first. After that we weren't two benches. We were one row of frightened fathers. When I opened the shop, I hired Ramdeo's nephew. I still love our Bengali songs. I just don't need anyone else to be less.

qa.q: Who had the only torch when the power went out?
qa.a: Ramdeo, a Bihari man.

qa.q: How did young Tanvir feel sitting on the Bengali bench at first?
qa.a: He felt at home and a little proud of "our bench", sitting with his own people without thinking.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows the us-them line loosening?
qa.a: Tanvir later hired Ramdeo's nephew at his shop, treating an outsider fairly while still loving Bengali songs.

qa.q: What might Ramdeo have felt, walking the torch down the corridor?
qa.a: He probably felt anxious like every waiting father, and wanted every mother and baby to be safe, not just those from his side.

grounding: A young father notices the pull to favour his own group in a hospital corridor, finds a wider shared identity as fathers and later treats outsiders fairly.
